title: External diseconomies of scale: congestion and factor prices

stages.name: External diseconomies of scale: congestion and factor prices
stages.title: External diseconomies of scale: congestion and factor prices
stages.sub: Two reasons a whole industry can face rising costs as it grows.

steps.q: A furniture-making town grows from 5 to 50 firms, all sending lorries out on the same small roads every day. As more firms join, do deliveries get faster or slower for everyone?
steps.hint: More lorries, same road space: what happens to traffic?
steps.pre: So more firms sharing the same roads causes

steps.q: Lorries now sit in queues for hours, wasting fuel and drivers' time. Does this raise or lower each firm's costs, even though no single firm caused it?
steps.right: It raises costs for every firm
steps.wrong: It only raises costs for the firm that joined last
steps.hint: The delay hits any lorry on that road, not just one firm's.

steps.q: All 50 furniture firms now need skilled carpenters, but the town only has enough for 20 firms' worth. As firms compete for the same small pool of carpenters, what happens to the wages firms must offer?
steps.hint: If many buyers chase a limited supply of workers, what happens to the price of hiring them?
steps.pre: So industry growth pushes up demand for

steps.q: Every firm in the town now pays higher wages for carpenters, and higher prices for timber too, purely because the whole industry expanded and competed for the same scarce inputs. Does this raise costs for one firm alone or for the industry as a whole?
steps.right: For the industry as a whole
steps.hint: The wage and timber price rises hit anyone buying those inputs, not just one firm.
